idiom_name: std::vector<Rule> with std::function conditions and actions
implementation_notes: There is no engine in the standard library, so the idiomatic C++ realization is a rule table: a vector of rule structs whose condition is std::function<bool(const Facts&)> and whose action is std::function<void(Facts&)>, populated with lambdas. C++11 is enough (lambdas, std::function, std::vector); std::variant plus if constexpr replaces the facts struct once facts become heterogeneous. Header-only third-party engines are the alternative when pattern matching over many facts, salience and refraction are needed - they buy the agenda semantics at the cost of a dependency, a DSL and dynamic typing at the engine boundary.
pitfalls: std::function erases the condition's type and its captures: a rule list kept beyond the lifetime of what a lambda captured by reference is a dangling-rule bug, and the type system will not flag it.
A table loaded from data (rule names, operators) loses all compile-time checking of fact fields, so it needs its own validation layer - with lambdas the checking is exactly what you give up.
An action that mutates the fields its own condition tests re-fires on the next pass unless 'fired' (or a cycle cap) stands in for refraction.

variants.name: Header-only C++17 Rete / behavior-tree engine
variants.idiom_name: rete_cpp / moar-rulez: header-only C++17 rule engines
variants.implementation_notes: When the rule set needs real pattern matching, header-only C++17 engines exist: rete_cpp builds a Rete network with alpha/beta memories, an agenda with conflict-resolution strategies and refraction behind a fluent add_rule().salience().when(...).then(...).build() API, while moar-rulez compiles a chain of rule lambdas into a behavior tree with operator overloading. They keep deployment simple (drop in a header, no build system change), but they are small third-party projects: pin a version, keep the rule definitions behind your own interface, and do not grow a rule base that only the engine can explain.
pitfalls: Facts become (identifier, attribute, value) triples: C++ types disappear at the engine boundary, so a typo'd attribute is a silently non-matching condition rather than a compile error.
Matching cost and Rete memory grow with the fact count; for a handful of rules the hand-written table is both simpler and faster.
Young header-only engines change their APIs: pin the version and wrap the engine so the rule base survives a swap.
